hero.title: Switch agents. Keep the context.
hero.lede: ai-memory is long-term memory for AI coding agents. Quit Claude Code mid-task, open Codex in the same directory, and carry on without re-explaining the architecture, the failed approaches or the open questions.

statement: Your coding agent already takes notes. They live on one machine and belong to one agent. Switch tools and they are gone, and your teammates never see them at all. ai-memory is what is on the other side of those walls.

continuity.label: What stays when everything else changes
continuity.title: Change everything. Keep what you know.

agents.title: Switch agents mid-task.
agents.text: Quit Claude Code, open Codex in the same directory. It starts with a handoff: what got done, what failed and what is still open.

machines.title: Switch machines.
machines.text: Memory lives in a small server you run: on your laptop, a homelab box, wherever. The project you left on the desktop is the project you resume on the notebook.
out: Two tests in auth_spec still fail.

team.title: Share it with your team.
team.text: Point everyone at one server. What one person’s sessions learn, everyone’s agents can find. New hires ask the project instead of interrupting you.

wiki.title: It writes its own wiki.
wiki.text: Hooks capture the work silently. Sessions become plain markdown pages, filed and cross-linked in a git-backed wiki. Grep it, open it in Obsidian, edit it by hand.

how.title: What happens while you work.
how.lede: All four steps run in the background, and the default path makes zero LLM calls.
how.figureAlt: Diagram: terminals emit observations that are consolidated into markdown pages, searched through fused ranking, and handed off to the next agent. Underneath it all sits a git-backed wiki of plain markdown files.

steps.title: Capture
steps.text: Lifecycle hooks record prompts, tool calls and session boundaries. Secrets are stripped before anything is stored.

steps.title: Consolidate
steps.text: When a session ends, its observations become a readable markdown page in the project’s wiki.

steps.title: Recall
steps.text: The next session gets a short brief and can search everything: full text, entities, links and vectors, fused into one ranking.

steps.title: Hand off
steps.text: The next session picks up the baton, and only one session can claim it. It works across agents and across every machine that reaches the server.

compare.title: Coming from another tool?
compare.text: Most memory tools need an LLM, a vector store or a graph database before they remember anything. ai-memory needs one binary and a folder.
compare.cta: Full comparison, including where they win
compare.pick: Pick the tool you use today

quickstart.title: Up and running in three commands.
quickstart.text: There is no sign-up. The default install listens on your machine only, so nothing else can reach it. You can add it to a project that is already under way: the first session imports the agent history you have on disk.

links.install: Every install path, step by step

solo.c1: 1. Install the binary (or grab it from the downloads page)
solo.c2: 2. Start the server. It listens on this machine only.
solo.c3: 3. Launch your agent through it. Hooks and MCP wire themselves.

community.title: Built in the open, by a lot of people.
community.text: New here? The contributing page shows where bug reports, pull requests and new agent integrations go.

aging.title: Old memory shrinks, and what you use stays.
aging.text: Session pages pile up for months. ai-memory scores them, keeps the ones you still read, and can compact or merge the rest with no LLM. An optional dream pass has your LLM merge cold pages while you are away, and every rewrite can be restored.
aging.figureAlt: Diagram: reading a page reinforces its retention score. The forget-sweep finds cold pages, which are evicted by default or, when enabled, compacted or merged into one survivor. Compacted and merged pages can be restored from git history.
